chapter_theme: The last twenty poems of the Purananuru are almost all bards' gate poems (கடைநிலை, இயன்மொழி, வாழ்த்தியல், பரிசில் விடை): a kinai or thadari drummer comes at dawn to a chief's gate, often driven by famine (Venus in the south), sings, and is answered by the same ritual of rags exchanged for fine cloth, toddy, meat and rice, after which he swears to sing no other patron. Their argument is that giving is the giver's glory and the bard's memory its return.

381.reading: After the bards had feasted long on meat and sweet milk-and-jaggery drinks and asked leave to go home, the chief of Venkatam, the son of the Karumban town man, afraid of their parting, told the kinai player that he would end his poverty and set him a sign to come back by after the summer rains, which the poet praises as a ferry that carries great and small in turn.
381.nuance: The chief fears the bard's leaving (எம்பிரிவு அஞ்சி), the word akam uses for lovers' separation, so the host-guest bond is spoken of as a bond of love. The opening quotation marks are unbalanced, so where the chief's speech begins (line 5 or line 15) is uncertain, and the simile of rain on a barren tangle (lines 8 to 10) may describe the wasted wealth of misers or the bard's wasted waiting.

thinai_evidence.note: a chief's speech of giving to a departing bard, told in praise of him

comparisons.tenor: the bard's labour at the gates of rich kings who do not give
the chief who carries great and small alike without forgetting

382.reading: The porunar declare they want only Nalankilli of the cool Chola land and will sing no other patron; fed and freed from hunger, the bard asks leave to go, saying the sea-girt world is the king's but his own part is to praise him in other kings' courts with his drum, so that his enemies tremble each time they hear it as the drumstick quivers each time it strikes.
382.nuance: The bard sells a service, not only thanks: praise sung in rival courts is to frighten the king's enemies. Lines 10 to 15 (the children who left, the snake shedding its skin) are hard to construe and one edition reads line 10 differently.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at a king's gate praising him and asking leave

comparisons.tenor: the clear eye of the kinai drum
the king's enemies trembling at each hearing of his praise

383.reading: Rising at cockcrow in the cold dawn, the bard beat his small drum at the long gate, blessed the bullocks and praised the chief, who clothed him in cloth fine as a snake's slough; reborn as it were, he will sing no other patron, since he has one man, Aviyan of the tall chariot, and need not fear whatever the drought-star Venus portends.
383.nuance: அழித்துப் பிறந்தனென் (line 16): the gift is felt as a second birth. The last line ties the bard's security to the patron against the omen of Venus, a motif this chapter repeats (384, 386, 388).

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at the gate who rests his life on one patron

384.reading: The kinai player describes the chief's land, where the heron sleeps on the vanji branch and the hare starts among the millet and farmers' bowls hold fish and toddy without a festival, and says that though he tried to stop him the chief kept giving paddy, gold and toddy, feeding with fat rice and ghee for fame; such a protector he had, so he knew only the day that came and never counted what was spent, whatever Venus foretold.
384.nuance: The colophon's thurai, கையறுநிலை, makes this a lament for a dead patron; the poem itself has only the past tense புரந்தோன் and அன்னோனை உடையேம் என்ப, which allows it but never says he is dead. The opening sets the soft wet land (மென் பாலான்) against the hard dry land (வன் பாலான்), both rich.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief's unstinting giving in a bard's voice

385.reading: The bard had not even come to his gate, but hearing his drum at another man's door at dawn, the lord of Ambar took pity, stripped off his earth-eaten rags, dressed him in white and ended his hunger; the poet wishes good Aruvanthai more years than the raindrops on Pulli's Venkatam.
385.nuance: The gift came unasked: the chief heard the drum at someone else's gate and called the bard in. புல்லிய (line 10) can be read as 'of Pulli', naming the chief of Venkatam whom akam poets also name, or as an epithet; the link to Akananuru 61 takes the first reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing for a patron who gave without being asked

comparisons.vehicle: வேங்கட விறல்வரைப் பட்ட ஓங்கல் வானத்து உறையினும் பலவே

386.reading: Killi Valavan gave so that his bards ate ghee-fried meat and milk food and knew the sweat of hot eating but never the sweat of work; his land holds paddy fields, herds with no bandits, ships counted under the punnai and salt traders on the backwaters, and his bards, who never fight, wish long life to the feet of the one who knew their want, whichever way Venus moves.
386.nuance: The four lands (வயலே, புறவே, கடலே, கழியே) are listed as one king's territory, a whole landscape in a single puram catalogue. பொரா அப் பொருநரேம், porunar who do not fight, plays on பொருநர் as both bard and warrior.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's gifts and the lands that feed them

comparisons.tenor: the ghee spattering from the frying meat

387.reading: The bard sang Chelvakkadungo Vazhiyathan as the king whose elephants break enemy walls and bring tribute that ends his supplicants' poverty; the king did not look down on the singer's smallness but gave by the measure of his own greatness elephants, horses, herds and fields so many that they seemed a dream given in waking, and the poet wishes him years more than the Porunai's sand and the paddy of its fields.
387.nuance: The poem names its own principle of measure: the gift is sized by the giver's greatness, not by the receiver's smallness (lines 20, 21). The list of gifts asked as questions (என்கோ) recurs in 396.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's praise and blessing of a Chera king's gift

comparisons.tenor: the years wished on the king

388.reading: When Venus stood in the south and the fields withered in a barren season, the drummer went to Pannan of Sirukudi, who saw his state and gave until his trouble fled; the bard swears that if he fails to sing Pannan every day, may the protection his kin have from Vazhuthi, the Pandya of the elephant army, fail.
388.nuance: The closing oath stakes the protection of a Pandya king on the bard's loyalty to a village landholder, so the small patron's gift binds the bard as firmly as a king's. Lines 8 to 11 (the tongue as ploughshare, the plough and the drum) can be construed more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's report of a landholder who fed him in famine

comparisons.tenor: the tongue of truthful speech used as a ploughshare

389.reading: Athanungan, lord of Venkatam where elephant calves are tied in the village common while their mothers grieve, gave to the young porunan asking only to be remembered when the drought dries the palmyra and the neem; the bard asks the patron he now addresses to give like Athanungan and end his family's hunger, so that the women of his house never hear the dirge at his gate.
389.nuance: The giver asks the receiver to remember him (எம்மும் உள்ளுமோ), so the patron himself treats the bard's memory as the return on the gift. The colophon names Athanungan as patron, though the poem holds him up as a model to a second patron it does not name.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard holds up one giver's words as a model to another patron

390.reading: At the guarded house that only well-wishers approach, the poet beat her drum for days; on the night she arrived the chief called the poor bard in, stripped the rag like old pond moss from her waist, dressed her in new cloth, served toddy and meat rice in silver vessels, sent red paddy in stacks to her family resting at the village common and told her to take it as plunder; kings with elephants do not even know such feeding.
390.nuance: கொண்டி, the word for war booty, is used for a gift: the bard is told to carry off the paddy as soldiers carry off plunder. The closing sets the chief above crowned kings, who cannot know such hunger-ending. The colophon gives Athiyaman; the poem does not name him, and lines 1 and 2 and the gap at line 26 are hard.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's account of a chief's feeding at his gate

comparisons.tenor: the yard of the chief's house

391.reading: When the northern land of Venkatam, rich in paddy and toddy feasts, fell into famine, the bard brought his large family south and asked in the old town for the house that relieves want; those who knew the chief recognised him as the poor porunan who had come before, so he has come to see the chief, and wishes him sweet sleep with his wife in his house among the punnai where herons roost, and fields that yield a thousandfold.
391.nuance: The bard's credentials are his known poverty: those who know the chief vouch for him because he came before and is still poor (lines 11 to 13). The blessing of rain at its time (துளிபதன் அறிந்து) answers the famine that drove him south.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard arrives at a patron's gate and blesses him

392.reading: At dawn at the gate of Ezhini of the Athiyar, the poet beat her one-eyed drum and hailed him as the daily ploughman who yokes donkeys on the bloody fields of conquered forts and sows white varagu and horse-gram; that day he took off her rags, clothed her in fine cloth, poured aged toddy into golden cups and gave food and a guest's share, the descendant of the one who brought sugarcane here like heaven's ambrosia.
392.nuance: The conqueror's destruction is sung as farming: donkeys plough the ruined fort and poor men's grains are sown where a city stood, a curse dressed as praise of his diligence (வைகல் உழவ). The sugarcane brought from heaven is the Athiyar house's own legend.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at the gate of a conqueror, praised and fed

comparisons.tenor: the king who lays waste enemy forts

393.reading: Wandering with his kin, their pots long empty and no one in other lands who knows the duty of feeding them, the bard came thinking of Killi Valavan's fame and asks him to end his family's hunger with fat meat heaped like summer cotton bales, to strip his rags and dress him in cloth like a new pakanrai flower and give lasting wealth, promising to beat his moon-white drum and sing the sword-true Valavan of the Kaviri land.
393.nuance: குடிமுறை பாடி (line 3): the bard's family sings lineages by inherited order, so asking is a hereditary office, not a lapse. Line 22 has a gap and is read differently in other editions.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's request for gifts at a king's gate

comparisons.vehicle: கோடைப் பருத்தி வீடுநிறை பெய்த மூடைப் பண்டம்
comparisons.tenor: the white fat meat asked for

394.reading: The poet warns other poets not to set their hopes on Kuttuvan, however the world praises his generosity: when he sang the king's father's war-song, Kuttuvan gave him a killer elephant; when the terrified bard sent it back, the king, ashamed it had seemed too small, gave a bigger one; so the bard will never go to his land again, however his family suffers.
394.nuance: Praise by mock complaint: the warning to poets is a boast that the gift outran anything a bard could use. The king reads the return of his gift as a judgment that it was too small (சிறிதென உணர்ந்தமை நாணி), so the giver's shame, not the receiver's need, sets the size of the second gift. வாடா வஞ்சி (line 9) names what the bard sang, a war-march song.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's giving in the mock form of a warning

395.reading: After a picture of Pidavur's rich fields, where farmers eat old rice with hare and fish and women drive off parrots, the bard says he is of Sathan's kin: arriving at dusk after a day on the hot road, he was given rare vessels at once, without delay or long speech, and the chief showed his wife and told her to care for him as for himself; since then the bard thinks of no one else, for even in drought the house keeps feeding him.
395.nuance: The chief makes his wife the bard's keeper (என்போல் போற்று), so the gift becomes a standing place in the household. The phrase 'not stopping, not saying much' (lines 27, 28) makes speed and few words part of the gift. The drought images of lines 33 to 35 show the giving does not depend on the season.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at a patron's gate recounts how he was received

comparisons.tenor: the long grains of cooked rice

396.reading: In Vattaru, where fish move in the low water and flowers like eyes bloom on the high, birds are driven off with drums and the Kosar dance the kuravai over toddy, Ezhiniyathan is strength to the weak and kin to the kinless; his kinai players list his roasts, toddy, hare-fat rice and open stores, say there is no bound to their wealth, and wish his fame to shine like the moon among the stars.
396.nuance: 'Strength to those without strength, kin to those without kin' (lines 10, 11) gives the chief's charity a social reach beyond bards. The list of foods in question form (என்கோ) is the same device as 387. Lines 21 and 22 have a gap.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's praise of a chief's land and table

comparisons.tenor: the flowers on the upper water

comparisons.vehicle: மீன் நாப்பண் விரி கதிர வெண் திங்களின்

397.reading: At dawn in the guarded war camp, when Venus rose and birds called and drums and conch sounded, the bard beat his drum and bade the garlanded king wake; pleased, Valavan gave him fried meat, fragrant toddy, cloth like a snake's slough and rare jewels, pouring like rain to end his summer heat, so the bard fears nothing even if the sea runs dry or the sun rises in the south, living in the cool shade of his feet.
397.nuance: The dawn song is a wake-up call in a war camp (ஏமப் பாசறை), so the bard serves the king's day as well as his fame. The final boast sets the patron's protection against cosmic upheaval, a claim of security that the ethics books would deny any wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's wake-up song in a camp and the gift that answered it

comparisons.tenor: the sacrificial fires of the brahmins
the protection of the king's feet

398.reading: At dawn, as the moon hid and Venus rose, cocks cried and bards played their lutes, the poet came to Vanjan of true word, whose old town is open to friends and shut to enemies like a cave where tigers sleep, and beat his drum asking that the king stay unfailing for them; glad at the small offering, the king took off the bard's rags, dressed him in cloth like rising smoke, filled a bowl like spat fire with clear toddy, fed his kin deer meat and rice, and gave the flowered cloth and gem necklace from his own body.
398.nuance: 'Rejoicing greatly at a small thing' (line 17) turns the usual scale: the king is grateful for the bard's coming. The cloth from the king's own body (புரையோன் மேனிப் பூந்துகில்) is the most intimate gift of the chapter. Line 2 has a gap, and பாயல் in the last line may be a place name.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's account of a Chera chief's dawn reception

comparisons.tenor: the town that enemies cannot approach

399.reading: After a picture of the rich Kaviri gardens of Killi Valavan, where field workers eat fish curry and boiled rice, the bard says he would go to no other face; living on bitter-gourd gruel his drum-wife cooked with fish from his own line, he sat apart in ruin, until, restringing his broken drum, he sang Thonrikkon as the most righteous and most valiant and asked only for a strong bullock for his cart, and before he had finished wanting it the chief gave a herd of many colours like stars with a cart.
399.nuance: The bard's own catch and his wife's gruel are counted as ruin (அழிவுகொண்டு), so living by one's own labour is the state the patron's gift rescues him from. How the opening picture of Valavan's land joins the gift of Thonrikkon is unclear (lines 12 to 14, a gap at line 8, line 26).

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's request and its fulfilment by a hill chief

400.reading: In the last watch of the night at full moon, the bard sounded his drum, round like the moon seen over the sea, and sang the king's lineage; the king, who stays awake while others sleep to guard the world, heard it and, still not satisfied, took away his old rag and gave fine vessels and cloth, so the bard is drunk on fresh toddy every day and has lost count of time; he drives off not only his own enemies but the hunger of those who come to him, lord of the town where ships are tied at every ford to the sacrificial post.
400.nuance: 'Hunger-enemy' (பசிப்பகை) sets the king's charity beside his wars as a second campaign of the same kind. The ships moored to the sacrificial post join trade and Vedic ritual in one image. Lines 12 and 18 have gaps.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's watchfulness and giving

comparisons.vehicle: வெண் திங்கள் மூ வைந்தான் முறை முற்றக், கடல் நடுவண் கண்ட

comparisons.tenor: hunger as an enemy to be driven off

links.note: Same poet, same patron (Karumbanur kizhan): 381 records the chief's own speech promising to end the bard's poverty; 384, under the thurai கையறுநிலை, says the bard knew only the day that came while the chief kept giving.
links.teaches: Read together the pair runs from promise to fulfilment and, if the colophon of 384 is right, to loss: the sign the chief set for the bard's return in 381 becomes in 384 a life lived without counting days, which is exactly what is exposed when such a protector dies.

links.note: Both by Kovur Kizhar for Nalankilli: 382 promises to sing the king in rival courts so his enemies tremble; 400 says he drives off both his enemies and the hunger of those who come to him.
links.teaches: The pair shows what the bard's paid praise carries: 382 offers fame as a weapon against the king's enemies, and 400 supplies its content, a king whose war and whose feeding are one campaign, so the gift buys propaganda for exactly the two powers it praises.

links.note: Avvaiyar at the gate of Athiyaman (390) and of his son Ezhini (392): the same stripping of rags, new cloth, toddy and food.
links.teaches: Father and son receive the same bard with the same ritual of rags exchanged for cloth, which shows the reception as an inherited house custom of the Athiyar rather than one chief's whim, while the son's poem adds conquest as the source of what is given.

links.note: 388 is the drummer's own account of Pannan of Sirukudi feeding him in famine; 173, ascribed to Killi Valavan, calls Pannan the physician of hunger and sends bards to his house.
links.teaches: A crowned Chola king and a starving drummer both name a village landholder as the remedy for hunger, and 388 binds the bard's loyalty to him by an oath on a Pandya's protection, so Pannan's fame for feeding crossed kingdoms and outranked kings in the bards' own reckoning.

links.note: Both by Kalladanar and both use Venkatam: 385 wishes a patron years more than the raindrops on Venkatam; 391 says the northern Venkatam land fell to famine and drove the bard south.
links.teaches: The same poet uses Venkatam's rain once as the measure of endless plenty and once as the place where the rain failed, so the hill stands in bardic poetry for the uncertainty of rain itself, which is why the bard's life follows the patron and not the land.

links.note: Akananuru 54 calls Pannan of Sirukudi one who does not live for himself but belongs to others, and sets the hero's homecoming by the gooseberries of his garden; 388 tells how Pannan fed a drummer in famine.
links.teaches: The akam poet can use Pannan's name as a byword for living for others without explaining it, which shows that the puram reputation 388 records was common knowledge by the time an akam homecoming could borrow it as a landmark.

links.note: 385 blesses Aruvanthai with years more than the raindrops on புல்லிய வேங்கட; Akananuru 61 names Pulli, the chief of the cattle raiders, as lord of the festive Venkatam where toddy is bartered for paddy.
links.teaches: If புல்லிய in 385 names Pulli, a bard of the south uses another chief's hill as the measure of his own patron's blessing, and akam remembers the same hill as a frontier reward the hero would not stay for, so Venkatam served both genres as the edge of the known Tamil world.

links.note: 389 describes Venkatam where a captured elephant calf is tied in the common while its mother grieves; Akananuru 83 shows Pulli's young men separating a calf from its wailing mother and tying it at the toddy houses of the Venkatam town.
links.teaches: The calf-taking scene was a fixed picture of Venkatam shared by both genres, and the pairing shows the akam hero's heart racing past a scene that the puram poet offers as plain proof of the lord's wealth, the same image put to opposite uses of distance and of plenty.

links.note: 395 places Pidavur east of Uranthai of Tittan of the small-eyed elephants; Akananuru 122 compares the many obstacles to secret love to the guarded walls of Tittan's Uranthai.
links.teaches: Tittan's Uranthai is a fixed point on both maps: puram uses it to locate a small chief's village and akam uses its fortifications as a measure of how hard a meeting is, so a king's fame became the grid by which smaller places and private feelings were placed.

links.note: 396 praises Ezhiniyathan of Vattaru, whose land has the toddy-drinking Kosar; Akananuru 216 names Athan Ezhini, lord of Selli, among whose people the young Kosar make garlands, and compares the parathai's pain to the elephant his spear pierced.
links.teaches: If the two Ezhinis are one chief (both are named with the Kosar), akam remembers him by a war wound inflicted on an elephant, used as a courtesan's image of suffering, while puram remembers him as feeder of the kinless, showing how a patron's two reputations were divided between the genres.

links.note: 386 praises the king because his bards knew only the sweat of eating hot food and never the sweat of work; Kural 1065 says nothing is sweeter than even thin gruel earned by one's own effort.
links.teaches: On the plain reading the two rank the same pair in opposite order: the bard's highest praise is to be spared labour by a giver, while the Kural makes self-earned food the sweetest, so the Kural's ethic of not asking is written against the very economy of patronage the Purananuru celebrates.

links.note: 399: the bard lived on bitter-gourd gruel his wife cooked with fish he caught himself and called it ruin (அழிவுகொண்டு) until the chief's gift came; Kural 1065: thin gruel from one's own effort is the sweetest food.
links.teaches: The poem gives the exact case the Kural imagines, gruel from one's own catch, and judges it the opposite way, as ruin to be ended by a patron, so the couplet is seen to argue against the bard's way of life and not merely in the abstract.

links.note: 393: the bard's family sings lineages by inherited order (குடிமுறை பாடி) and asks the king for food and cloth; Kural 1062 curses the maker of the world if anyone must live by begging.
links.teaches: What the Kural treats as an outrage against the world's order, a life that depends on asking, the bard presents as a hereditary office with its own proper order of song, so the two disagree on whether living by the gift is a shame or a calling.

links.note: 389: as he gives, Athanungan asks the bard whether he will remember him in the drought; Kural 1059: what renown would givers have without people who ask?
links.teaches: The Kural states abstractly that the giver's fame needs the asker; the poem shows a giver who knows it, asking to be remembered as he gives, so the bard's memory is the very return the giver seeks.

links.note: 395: the chief shows his wife to the bard and tells her to care for him as for himself; Kural 81: the whole of keeping house and guarding goods is for tending guests.
links.teaches: The couplet says the household exists for the guest; the poem shows the moment that claim is enacted, when the master hands the guest over to the mistress of the house, so the guest is taken into the household rather than merely fed by it.

links.note: 394: Kuttuvan gives a killer elephant, and when the frightened bard returns it gives a bigger one, ashamed the first seemed small; Kural 221: true giving is giving to those who have nothing.
links.teaches: The Kural defines a gift by the receiver's want, but Kuttuvan's elephants are sized to the giver's honour and are useless to a hungry bard, so the poem shows a royal giving that the Kural's definition would hardly count as ஈகை at all.

links.note: 387: the king did not look at the bard's smallness but gave by the measure of his own greatness; Kural 87: the fruit of hospitality has no set measure, being as great as the guest's worth.
links.teaches: The Kural measures hospitality by the guest's worth, while the poem praises a king precisely for ignoring the guest's low worth and measuring by his own, so royal giving runs on a scale opposite to the household's.

links.note: 400: besides driving off his own enemies, the king can drive off the hunger-enemy of those who come to him; Kural 225: the strength to bear hunger ranks behind the strength to remove others' hunger.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks hunger-removal above ascetic endurance as a kind of strength; the poem makes it a second warfare of the king, so the couplet's ranking appears to draw on a heroic vocabulary in which feeding was counted as victory.

links.note: 397: under the king's protection the bard will fear nothing even if the sea ends or the sun rises in the south; Naladiyar 1: those who once ate six-flavoured food may go begging for gruel, so wealth cannot be counted as lasting.
links.teaches: The bard claims a security from his patron that survives cosmic upheaval, while the Naladiyar denies that any wealth or provision lasts, so the two make incompatible claims about whether a gift can make a life safe.

new_concepts.gloss: the helpless grief of those left behind at a patron's or hero's death
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon thurai of 384 names it

new_concepts.gloss: the small drum of the porunar bards, and the bard who beats it at the patron's gate

382 line 10 is the edition variant the flag records; line 12 யங்கேள் and line 13 கட்கேள்விக் look corrupt; the review's table says our text lacks a line the site has (site line 11).
383: lines 14, 15, 19 and 20 are gaps; we have 23 lines against 25 in Duraisamy Pillai's edition, and the review notes the site breaks the lines differently.
384: lines 5, 10 and 13 are gaps (line 5 is full in one edition); line 10 repeats in 396 line 14; the review notes the site breaks the lines differently.
